fatal_errors: The proposed compositional substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention of cold rolling followed by controlled recovery/recrystallization annealing.
The cited evidence supports the general Mo-strength/Nb-ductility tradeoff but does not establish that Mo reduction in NbZrTiHfMo will retain at least 90% of its 1719 MPa compressive yield strength.

The substitution amount is ambiguously expressed: reducing Mo by 10–20 at.% could mean an absolute reduction from its original 20 at.% or a 10–20% relative reduction, whereas the experiment uses the latter.
explanation: The hypothesis directly addresses the requested room-temperature strength–plasticity problem and offers a coherent, testable alternative based on reducing Mo and increasing Nb. E2 provides relevant qualitative support that Mo favors strength while Nb favors ductility, but neither cited source validates the claimed electronegativity/lattice-distortion mechanism or the quantitative expectation of minimal strength loss in this alloy. It differs fundamentally from the hidden target, which used a strongly nonequiatomic Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 alloy and microstructural control by 20–80% cold rolling and 650–800 °C annealing. The target mechanism involved work hardening, dislocation walls, boundary and texture strengthening, followed by recovery and partial recrystallization; these conditions and mediators are absent. The proposed composition-series experiment is nevertheless decisive because it measures phase retention, yield strength, and strain to failure against explicit falsification thresholds.
